DEFECT-DETECTOR DISCIPLINE (overrides any "assessment=GOOD" rule below): this practice catches a specific defect — copy-pasted near-identical logic. What would be PRESENT for it is the defect, so (outcome occurrence=PRESENT, assessment=GOOD) is never available here: it would read as an endorsement of a good act nobody observed.

A clean result is still a real result, and it has the other shape. This practice judges ONE closed corpus — the lines this PR ADDS — and a flaggable pair must sit inside it, so once you have read every added hand-written hunk and no near-identical pair is in them, you have PROVEN something rather than merely failed to find it: (outcome occurrence=ABSENT, assessment=GOOD), the copy-paste that could have appeared in this change did not. Record it with evidence.exhaustiveSearch over scm.pull-request.diff, name in boundary that duplication against code outside the diff is out of scope either way, and cite the repeated-looking blocks you actually checked. Note that this is NOT the unverifiable claim the old refusal was aimed at: you are not certifying that no duplicate of this code exists anywhere in the repository — which you could never see — only that the added lines do not duplicate one another, which is exactly the question this practice asks.

So three verdicts, plus one abstention. (outcome occurrence=PRESENT, assessment=BAD) when you can quote a near-identical added pair. (outcome occurrence=ABSENT, assessment=GOOD) when you read the added hand-written lines through and no such pair is there. NO_REVIEW_OCCASION only when the change offers no surface to judge at all — a docs/config-only diff, or one whose added lines are entirely generated, vendored, or test fixtures — because that value says the work had no subject here, which is false of a diff you read and found clean. The one further answer available to you is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, for a candidate pair you read and genuinely cannot call.

THE STANDARD. A senior reviewer flags copy-paste: two or more added blocks that are near-identical in shape and differ only in a few literals, identifiers, or types — the kind of repetition an Extract Function, a shared constant, a loop, or a small lookup table would collapse into one source of truth (Fowler; Hunt & Thomas, DRY; Martin). The harm is drift: a fix has to land in every copy, and the copy you forget becomes the bug. Judge the repeated *unit* of knowledge (the same computation or rule expressed twice), not text that merely looks alike: a coherent multi-line computation, validation, mapping/transform, or constant/config block can be a flaggable copy; a one-liner, a guard clause, a field assignment, or a forced-similar idiom (equals/hashCode, builder chains, switch arms, DI/route registrations) is not. Use your judgment about whether two blocks are a genuine copy-paste or merely a coincidental shared idiom. When the pair that would decide this practice is one you genuinely cannot call from the added lines, say INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE and quote it — do not resolve the doubt into a finding, and do not resolve it into NO_REVIEW_OCCASION either, which claims there was nothing here to look at.

WHAT IS / ISN'T IN SCOPE. Judge only the lines this PR ADDS (the [L<n>] new-side spans in added hunks); pre-existing duplication you cannot see being introduced here is out of scope. Repetition that is *legitimately* parallel is not a defect: test cases, fixtures, and table-driven/parametrized bodies are meant to look alike; generated or vendored output (*.gen.*, lockfiles, OpenAPI specs, route trees, migrations, and the like) is not hand-written — assess only the hand-authored remainder. This practice judges REPETITION across blocks only; whether one block is too long or does too many things belongs to keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose — never flag a single block here.

ASSESSMENT & SEVERITY (philosophy, not a lookup table). Non-blocking and formative: a habit to grow, never a merge gate, and capped at MAJOR on this signal alone. Calibrate to consequence and spread, as a reviewer would: a duplicated pure-UI/markup block with no logic is a gentle "extract a component" nudge; duplicated LOGIC where a divergent copy is a real bug risk weighs more; a copy already spreading to several places or several distinct duplicated blocks warrants the upper end. Identical added code must always yield identical severity.

GROUNDING & STANCE. Every BAD finding must quote BOTH occurrences by their [L<n>] spans and path and name the small delta between them; a duplication claim you cannot ground in two quoted added spans is not made. Describe only the observable copy-paste habit — never assert the code is buggy, will diverge, or will break, and never impute intent or character. Look before you leap: scan the added blocks for genuine structural sameness before flagging or abstaining by either route — duplication can live WITHIN one function too: sibling `if`/`case`/branch bodies that each repeat the same multi-line computation differing only in a constant are as flaggable as cross-function copies, so inspect branch bodies, not just whole functions, before abstaining. When no near-identical added pair is quotable, which answer you owe depends on whether there was anything to read: clean non-duplicated hand-written logic you scanned through is (ABSENT, GOOD) with its search recorded, while a docs/config-only diff or one dominated by generated/vendored/test surface had no subject for this practice and is NO_REVIEW_OCCASION.
practices.whyItMatters: Copy-pasted logic means every future fix has to land in every copy, and the copy you forget keeps the old behaviour, which is exactly the bug. Pull the shared part into one place and you fix it once.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: By the time the same validation logic shows up a third time, you stop copying it and lift the shared concept into one named helper every caller uses, leaving a single source of truth instead of copies that drift apart. You hold off when blocks only look alike by coincidence, since forcing a shared abstraction on them is worse than the duplication.

practices.name: Keep functions small and single-purpose
practices.criteria:
DEFECT-DETECTOR DISCIPLINE (overrides any 'assessment=GOOD' rule below): this practice catches a specific defect — a single added function body that sprawls across many separable responsibilities or buries its core action under deep nesting. What would be PRESENT for it is that defect, so (PRESENT, GOOD) is never available here: endorsing it would be a whole-function cohesion and correctness bill of health you cannot stand behind from the diff alone, since the function's collaborators and the responsibilities it delegates live outside the added lines.

A clean result is a different claim, and one you CAN make. The shape of a body is visible in the body — its length, its nesting, the concerns written out in it — and the bodies this change introduces are a closed set you can enumerate from the diff. So when you have read every added or substantially rewritten body and none sprawls, nests deeply, or interleaves separable concerns, that is (outcome occurrence=ABSENT, assessment=GOOD): the sprawl that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with evidence.exhaustiveSearch over scm.pull-request.diff, say in boundary that you judged shape and not whether the functions are correct or well-factored against collaborators you cannot see, and cite the largest body you read. Keep NO_REVIEW_OCCASION for a change that adds no function body at all — a value that says the work had no subject here, which is untrue of a change whose bodies you read and found focused.

THE STANDARD. A senior reviewer asks of the largest function the change introduces or substantially rewrites: can I hold its purpose in my head, name it in a phrase, and follow it at a glance? A focused function does one nameable job. The defect is a single body that visibly interleaves several SUBSTANTIAL, separable concerns (each a real multi-step block, genuinely interwoven — not a short serialize/encode/respond tail on a coherent pipeline), OR nests control flow so deep the core action is lost in indentation, OR runs so long its purpose stops being scannable. Reason like an expert about THIS code's shape; do not apply a line count or a fixed concern count, and never quote any threshold to the developer.

GOOD vs BAD, by example (open, non-exhaustive). NOT a defect: a linear pipeline of single-purpose stages (guard → build → encode → return; validate → operate → respond) is ONE purpose even when it ends by serializing a result; a thin body that delegates each step to a named helper in one call each (parse → fetch → render) is ONE orchestration — the responsibilities live in the helpers, so counting one-line delegated calls as separate concerns is the false positive to avoid. A defect: one body that parses input AND performs I/O AND applies business rules AND formats output, each written out and tangled together; or a handler whose real action sits four conditionals deep. Use your judgment for cases these examples don't cover.

PRESENCE / ASSESSMENT / SEVERITY. Three verdicts: (PRESENT, BAD) with a quotable offending body; (ABSENT, GOOD) when you read the added bodies through and none carries the defect; NO_REVIEW_OCCASION when the change adds no body that could carry the defect at all. The one further answer available to you is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, for a body you can see is large but whose shape the diff truncates before you can judge it. Grade the single most consequential function, never sum across files, and never escalate because many separate small functions exist — many small focused units IS the baseline. Stay non-blocking: this is a craft habit about how work is shaped, never a correctness claim, and it never exceeds MAJOR on function shape alone. Reserve the top of that ceiling for a body that clearly does it all or whose core action is genuinely obscured by nesting; use the lower rung when a reader can still follow it and a single extraction would help.

GROUNDING + STANCE. Every BAD finding must quote the specific [L<n>] added span and name the responsibilities to split out or the nesting to flatten; a sprawl you cannot anchor to a quoted hunk is not emittable — when the body that would decide it is truncated in the diff, say INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE; otherwise return NO_REVIEW_OCCASION instead of inventing one. Judge only function bodies visible in the diff; never reason about an unchanged caller or a function merely renamed or called but not shown. If the diff is docs/config-only, pure deletion or rename, or dominated by generated/vendored files with essentially no hand-written body to judge, return NO_REVIEW_OCCASION. Describe the observable shape; never impute intent or character.

DEFER. Repeated/near-identical blocks belong to removes-duplication; dead, commented-out, or leftover scaffolding belongs to leaves-code-clean. If the only shape concern is duplication or dead code, this practice is NO_REVIEW_OCCASION.
practices.whyItMatters: A function that does five things is hard to name, hard to test, and hard to change without breaking a part you forgot it touched. Small, focused functions are the ones you can actually hold in your head.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Instead of one long method that parses, validates, saves, and notifies, you have a few short functions, each doing one clearly named step you can read and test on its own.

practices.name: Leave the code clean and comment the why
practices.criteria:
DEFECT-DETECTOR DISCIPLINE: this practice hunts for a specific defect — residue left behind on added lines. What would be PRESENT for it is that residue, so (PRESENT, GOOD) is never available here: "the code is clean" as a general endorsement is a bill of health nobody can write.

But this practice judges a corpus you are handed WHOLE — the added lines of this diff, every one of them, marked as such — and residue is visible in the line itself. So "I read all the added lines and none carries a blemish" is not a lucky miss, it is a covered search, and it is (outcome occurrence=ABSENT, assessment=GOOD): the residue that could have shipped with this change did not. Record it with evidence.exhaustiveSearch over scm.pull-request.diff, and use boundary to say exactly what you did NOT cover — unchanged lines, files this diff does not touch, generated and vendored surface — so the claim reaches no further than the reading behind it.

Three verdicts, then. (PRESENT, BAD) with a quotable blemish on an added line. (ABSENT, GOOD) when you read the added hand-written lines through and none carries one. NO_REVIEW_OCCASION only when there were no hand-written added lines to read — an all-generated or all-vendored diff — since that value claims the work had no subject here. The one further answer available to you is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, for a single candidate line you read and genuinely cannot call.

STANDARD: code that ships clean and comments that earn their place. A senior reviewer scanning the added lines should find no residue from the writing process — no commented-out code, no leftover debug/trace output, no throwaway scaffolding shipped as if final — and any comment that IS present should explain the WHY (intent, a non-obvious constraint, a unit, a caveat, a reference) rather than merely restate the WHAT the very next line already says.

GOOD vs BAD (open, illustrative — reason about cases not listed):
- BAD, e.g. an added line that is itself plausible source behind a comment marker (a commented-out assignment, call, or control statement); a bare trace print or breakpoint left in shipped code; a "TEMP/remove-before-merge" stub; a comment like "// increment i" above i++ that adds nothing.
- GOOD/clean, e.g. a comment giving a reason ("retry once: upstream drops the first call after idle"); output that is the file's deliberate purpose (a CLI's own stdout, a test's expected-output); a logger call through a real logging facility; a sanctioned TODO referencing a tracked issue. When the prose comment that would decide this practice is one you genuinely cannot call — restatement or explanation — do not resolve the doubt in either direction: quote it and answer INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. That applies ONLY to prose. Commented-out source is never an explanatory comment: if the text after the comment marker would itself parse as code in this file's language (it opens with a control/declaration keyword such as `case`/`if`/`guard`/`for`/`while`/`return`/`func`/`let`/`var`, or is an assignment or a `name(...)` call — especially when an identical live statement appears elsewhere in the diff), it is commented-out code (PRESENT, BAD), not a WHY comment.

GROUNDING & CONTEXT BOUNDARY: judge ONLY lines the diff marks as ADDED (leading '+'); removed and unchanged lines are not graded — code the author commented out and DELETED is a cleanup, never a blemish. Quote the exact [L<n>] span and file path for every blemish; a blemish you cannot quote is not counted. Never infer that a line is dead or debug-only unless its quoted text shows it. Exclude generated/vendored files (lockfiles, *.gen.*, specs, build output, migrations) — if no hand-written added surface remains, or the diff is empty, emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION; if the diff is truncated where the added lines live, emit INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE instead.

SEVERITY (principle, not a counter): this is cosmetic residue with no functional impact, so it is a gentle, NON-BLOCKING nudge — never a merge gate, and never exceeds MAJOR on this practice alone. A lone stray comment or marker is the lightest touch; a scatter of leftovers is a modest cleanup; reserve the top of the range for residue with real bite — e.g. a debug print left inside an otherwise-empty catch, where swallowed handling crosses into functional risk. Sheer line count does not raise severity: a long commented-out block is still one cleanliness nudge. Identical added lines must yield identical severity.

DEFER: this practice judges only residue-on-added-lines and WHAT-vs-WHY comments. It does NOT judge naming, function/file size, scope, duplication, dead branches in live code, swallowed errors, or runtime defects — sibling practices own those; do not borrow their complaint.

STANCE: describe the observable behaviour — what the author left behind in the code — never impute intent or character.
practices.whyItMatters: Stray debug output, blocks of commented-out code, and comments that just echo the line all add noise the next reader has to wade through. Clean code with a comment that explains the why reads like someone meant it.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: No leftover print statements or commented-out branches, and where a line looks surprising, a short comment gives the reason, such as 'retry once: the upstream API drops the first call after an idle period', rather than restating what the line does.

groups.name: Handling failure well
groups.description: Fail safely when things go wrong. Handle errors instead of swallowing them, check inputs and edge cases where data enters, and do not crash on a problem the code could recover from.

practices.name: Handle errors instead of swallowing them
practices.criteria:
DEFECT-DETECTOR DISCIPLINE (overrides any "assessment=GOOD" rule below): this practice catches a specific defect — a failure that is caught or received and then silently dropped. What would be PRESENT for it is that swallow, so (PRESENT, GOOD) is never available here: it would be a clean bill of health on logic whose correctness you cannot verify, and correctness is not yours to certify.

The clean result is a narrower claim, and it is one you can make. Swallowing is VISIBLE — an empty catch, an unused error variable, an ignored return — and the failure paths this change adds are a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines. So when you have walked every added failure path and each one propagates, records, or is deliberately absorbed with a stated why, that is (outcome occurrence=ABSENT, assessment=GOOD): the swallow that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with evidence.exhaustiveSearch over scm.pull-request.diff, and say in boundary what you did NOT establish — that the handling is CORRECT, that the recovery works, that paths outside the diff behave — so the strength stays a claim about what is visibly there and not a warranty.

So three verdicts. PRESENT+BAD for a quotable swallowed failure. (ABSENT, GOOD) when the change adds failure paths and none of them swallows. NO_REVIEW_OCCASION ONLY when the change adds no failure path at all — that value says this work had no subject for the practice, and saying it about a developer who wrote sound error handling tells them there was nothing here to see. The one further answer available to you is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, for a failure path you can see whose handling the diff does not show you.

STANDARD: When this change introduces a failure path — a call that can throw, reject, or return an error — the failure should stay visible: surfaced to a caller who can react, or recorded with enough context that someone can diagnose it later. The defect this practice names is a failure that is caught or received and then SILENTLY DROPPED, so downstream code carries on with bad or missing data and no one learns it failed. A handler that records the failure but then lets downstream code proceed on the missing or bad value is still this defect (the error was detected, then no corrective action taken), not an acquittal. Judge this as a craft habit in how the ADDED code handles errors, not a line-by-line lint sweep.

CLEAN (→ ABSENT, GOOD once you have walked every added failure path): the error propagates (rethrows, wraps with context, returns/forwards it), is recorded meaningfully (logged at a level a human would notice, a failure metric, an error state the UI reads), or is deliberately absorbed with an in-diff comment naming WHY that is safe. BAD (→ PRESENT): the failure is discarded — e.g. an empty or no-op catch, a caught error variable that is never used, an ignored error return, a dropped async rejection. These are illustrations, not a closed list; recognise the same shape in any language or idiom using your judgment as an experienced reviewer.

SEVERITY (non-blocking, formative — a habit to grow, never a merge gate; never exceeds MAJOR): a swallow on a best-effort or clearly secondary path (cleanup, teardown, optional telemetry, or merely logged a touch too quietly) is MINOR; a swallow that hides a real fault from the caller or user — on a path that persists, communicates, authenticates, parses, or otherwise carries consequence — is MAJOR. Multiple distinct swallows lean MAJOR. Identical constructs must yield identical severity. Name the single most consequential swallowed failure, not an exhaustive list.

PROCESS STANCE: before abstaining either way, actually scan the added hunks for failure paths and check where each error goes — don't assume a clean surface from a glance. INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE is not a shortcut around that scan: it is what you say after it, when the handling of a path you did find is genuinely not shown to you.

GROUNDING (mandatory): judge only constructs this diff ADDS or MODIFIES (new-side [L<n>] markers); never grade pre-existing context or assume code you cannot see. Per-commit patches are not in your context — reason from what the diff shows. Every PRESENT finding must quote the exact added hunk that shows the discard; if you cannot point to the dropped error in a quoted added line, you do not have a finding. If the hand-written change adds no failure path at all, emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION and name that fact. If it does add one but the relevant diff is truncated or unavailable, emit INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE — you could not read the handling, which is not the same as there being none. Never invent a construct, an exoneration, or a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the observable behaviour; never impute intent or character.

DEFER: this practice does not judge whether inputs/edge cases are validated (validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary), nor a deliberate fail-fast crash on an unrecoverable state (avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes) — those are sibling practices.
practices.whyItMatters: An empty catch block turns a failure into a silent one: the code carries on as if nothing went wrong, and you find out only when something downstream breaks with no clue why. Surfacing the error saves the 2am debugging session.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A failed call either surfaces the error to a caller who can react or recovers safely, for example by rolling back the partial work and failing closed, instead of logging and then continuing (or silently continuing) with bad or missing data.

practices.name: Validate inputs and edge cases at the boundary
practices.criteria:
DEFECT-DETECTOR DISCIPLINE: this practice exists to catch one specific defect — a boundary value consumed with no guard on the obvious failure case. What would be PRESENT for it is that unguarded consumption, so (PRESENT, GOOD) is never available here: it would be a clean bill of health on logic whose correctness you cannot execute or verify.

A clean result is the other verdict, and it is provable over the corpus this practice actually ranges over. The consuming sites this change introduces are a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines, and whether each meets a guard is visible in those same lines. So when you have walked every introduced consuming site and each handles its obvious bad case, that is (outcome occurrence=ABSENT, assessment=GOOD): the unguarded boundary that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with evidence.exhaustiveSearch over scm.pull-request.diff, and state in boundary what you did NOT establish — that the guards are SUFFICIENT, that they cover every case, that callers beyond the diff are safe — so the strength claims coverage of your reading and nothing about correctness.

Three verdicts, then. (PRESENT, BAD) for a quotable instance of the defect. (ABSENT, GOOD) when the change introduces consuming sites and each one is guarded. NO_REVIEW_OCCASION only when the change consumes no boundary value at all, since that value claims the work had no subject here. The one further answer available to you is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, for a consuming site you can see whose guard the visible context does not settle.

THE STANDARD. Judge whether added or modified code that consumes a value it does not control handles the obvious failure case on purpose, instead of assuming a happy path. A boundary value is one entering from outside the local logic — a request param/body/header, a parsed string or number, a value fetched by key or index from a collection, a file/stream/env/config read, the result of a third-party or RPC call. A site is in scope only when the same change also USES that value: dereferences it, indexes it, computes on it, or passes it into logic that assumes a shape. A value merely forwarded untouched, or one whose shape its type already guarantees, is not a boundary-consuming site. This is the defensive-programming habit at module boundaries (McConnell; SEI CERT input-validation): does the obvious failure case meet a guard, or a crash three layers deep?

CLEAN (→ ABSENT, GOOD once you have walked every introduced consuming site) looks like: each introduced consuming site handles the obvious bad case — a null/empty/missing-key check, a try/catch or error-return around a parse that can fail, a bounds check before indexing, a range/sign/finite check before arithmetic, a default for an absent config, or a framework guard visible in the same hunk (e.g. a Bean Validation annotation, an early return on the bad case). Judge the HABIT — is the obvious failure handled at all — not an exhaustive lint of every conceivable input. BAD looks like: a site reads an uncontrolled value and then dereferences/indexes/computes on it with no guard in the same hunk or its immediate visible context, so a malformed or absent input breaks the new path.

SEVERITY (non-blocking, formative). A single unguarded site is MINOR; several unguarded introduced sites is MAJOR. Never exceed MAJOR on this practice alone — it is a habit to grow, not a merge gate. Describe the observable code behaviour; never impute intent or character. Identical hunks must yield identical severity; use your judgment as an experienced reviewer for everything in between.

GROUNDING / ANTI-FABRICATION. Judge only the added/modified lines and their visible in-diff context ([L<n>] new-side markers); per-commit and surrounding code outside the diff are not in your context — never claim to run, compile, or test it. Before concluding, actually scan the changed lines for an uncontrolled value that gets consumed — look before you leap. A (PRESENT, BAD) finding REQUIRES quoting the exact [L<n>] span of each unguarded site and naming the missing guard (e.g. "null check before .name", "catch around the parse"). Never assert a missing guard you cannot point to: when the consuming site that would decide this practice is one whose guard could plausibly sit just above a truncated hunk, answer INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE rather than resolving the doubt into either a finding or a claim that no boundary surface was here. If the diff is empty, consumes no boundary input, or only generated/vendored files remain, emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION — never invent an input surface or a clean bill of health.

DEFER. This judges robustness against malformed/absent/out-of-range input only — not whether untrusted input reaches a dangerous sink unescaped (a sibling security practice), and not the quality of error handling once input is guarded (a sibling error practice; a catch that merely prevents the crash satisfies the guard here regardless of its body). When a hunk's only defect belongs to a sibling, abstain rather than co-flag.
practices.whyItMatters: Data from a user, a file, or another service will not always arrive in the shape you expected: it can be empty, null, negative, or huge. Checking it where it enters means a clear rejection instead of a confusing crash three layers deep.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Code that reads an external value first asks what happens if it is missing or out of range and handles that on purpose, so an empty list or a malformed payload meets a clean guard instead of a null-pointer surprise.

practices.name: Avoid crashing on recoverable problems
practices.criteria:
DEFECT-DETECTOR DISCIPLINE (overrides any "assessment=GOOD" rule below): this practice catches one specific defect — a construct that hard-stops the process on a condition an ordinary program could survive. What would be PRESENT for it is that chosen crash, so (PRESENT, GOOD) is never available here: it would be a clean bill of health on logic whose correctness you cannot verify.

A clean result is a different and reachable claim. A chosen crash is SHAPED — a force-unwrap, a force-cast, a deliberate abort — and the crash-shaped constructs this change adds are a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines. So when you have read every one of them and each sits on a genuine programmer invariant rather than an ordinary runtime path, that is (outcome occurrence=ABSENT, assessment=GOOD): the chosen crash that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with evidence.exhaustiveSearch over scm.pull-request.diff, and say in boundary that you judged the constructs the diff adds and not whether unchanged code can still crash, so the claim reaches exactly as far as your reading.

Three verdicts, then. (PRESENT, BAD) with a quoted instance. (ABSENT, GOOD) when the change adds crash-shaped constructs and none of them is a chosen crash. NO_REVIEW_OCCASION only when the change adds no crash-shaped construct at all, since that value claims the work had no subject here. The one further answer available to you is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, for a construct you can see whose value provenance the diff does not settle.

STANDARD. Code should degrade gracefully on ordinary, recoverable runtime failure rather than deliberately aborting. A "chosen crash" is an added construct that hard-stops the process on a condition an ordinary program could survive — force-unwrapping/force-casting a value that can legitimately be absent, or a deliberate abort/panic/exit/fatal-error — when that value rides an ordinary runtime path (parsed input, network/DB/disk/env, decoded payload, a fallible API's result). Judge whether the failure was recoverable and whether the author chose to crash on it anyway. Use your judgment as an experienced reviewer across languages and stacks; do not lean on a fixed list of keywords.

GOOD vs BAD (open examples, not a checklist). Bad, e.g.: force-unwrapping a value decoded from JSON or fetched from a server; panicking on a fallible parse; calling a fatal abort on a path that could return an error instead. Acceptable — not a chosen crash — e.g.: a genuine programmer invariant that cannot hold unless surrounding code is already broken (an unreachable enum default, a precondition on a value just proven non-nil); a fail-fast at a CLI/startup entry point where aborting IS the contract; an operation that is total by language contract for its operand type and provably cannot fail; force-unwrapping an author-controlled literal/constant. Reason about totality and provenance, not the spelling of the construct.

PROCESS STANCE. Before abstaining either way, actually scan the added lines for crash-shaped constructs and trace where each crashed-on value came from — look before you leap. INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE is earned by that trace running out of evidence, never by skipping it. A crash you cannot tie to a runtime-sourced value is not groundable.

PRESENCE / ASSESSMENT / SEVERITY (principles, not a lookup table). PRESENT, BAD only when you can quote the deciding added line and name the runtime source of the value it crashes on. Decide by whether the operation can ACTUALLY return nil/throw on some real input, not by the mere presence of `!`/force-unwrap: a conversion that is total by language contract (e.g. Swift `String.data(using: .utf8)` for a Unicode-capable encoding, or indexing a literal-bounded array) provably cannot fail, so it is not this defect and never a finding — it is one of the constructs a clean (ABSENT, GOOD) pass reports having read. Severity then scales with how clearly the failure was recoverable and how ordinary the source is: a clear recoverable runtime source warrants the ceiling; genuine uncertainty about recoverability lowers it — and when you cannot demonstrate a concrete input on which the unwrapped operation yields nil, do not exceed MINOR. This finding is non-blocking and NEVER exceeds MAJOR on its own. Identical hunks must yield identical severity.

GROUNDING + ANTI-FABRICATION. Cite the exact added-line span and the value's origin from observable diff evidence. Never invent a file, line, value source, or clean bill you did not verify. If a crash-shaped construct is visible but the fact that would settle it is not, return INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. Judge only added/modified lines (each carries an [L<n>] new-side marker); never reason about removed lines or code outside the diff, and never claim to compile or run it. CONTEXT BOUNDARY: you see the diff, not the whole program — when you cannot see enough to know whether the value a visible crash-construct acts on is runtime-sourced and recoverable, that construct is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE: you read it and it does not decide. Never guess, and never file it under NO_REVIEW_OCCASION, which claims no such construct was here. Docs/config/data-only or generated/vendored-only diffs carry no surface — NO_REVIEW_OCCASION.

NON-BLOCKING / NO INTENT. Frame this as a defensive-programming habit to grow, describing the observable behaviour of the code; never impute intent or character.

DEFER. Empty/swallowed catches, logged-and-continued errors, and missing input validation belong to sibling practices — judge only the deliberate-crash construct here.

FEED-FORWARD. When BAD, name the single most consequential chosen crash and show the shape of the graceful alternative for that line (guard/if-let, try-with-fallback, return-an-error, Result); do not rewrite the whole change.
practices.whyItMatters: Reaching for a force-unwrap or a panic on a condition that can actually happen turns an ordinary hiccup into a hard crash for your users. A problem the code can recover from deserves a graceful path, not a deliberate stop.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Where a value might legitimately be absent, the code unwraps it safely and falls back to a default or a clear error, instead of force-unwrapping and bringing the whole thing down.

groups.name: Making changes secure by default
groups.description: Make each change secure by default. Validate and escape untrusted input before it reaches a dangerous sink, avoid insecure defaults and over-broad permissions, and change dependencies deliberately.

practices.name: Neutralize untrusted input before a dangerous sink
practices.criteria:
DEFECT-DETECTOR DISCIPLINE (overrides any "assessment=GOOD" rule below): this practice exists to catch a specific defect — an untrusted value reaching a dangerous sink raw. What would be PRESENT for it is that flow, so (PRESENT, GOOD) is never available here: it would be a clean bill of health on logic whose correctness you cannot fully verify.

A clean result is the other verdict, and it is admissible over the corpus this practice bounds. The source-to-sink flows this change introduces are a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines, and whether each is parameterized, escaped, or allow-listed is visible in those same lines. So when you have traced every introduced flow and each is neutralized before its sink, that is (outcome occurrence=ABSENT, assessment=GOOD): the injection that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with evidence.exhaustiveSearch over scm.pull-request.diff, and state in boundary what you did NOT establish — that the escaping is CORRECT for every input, that sinks reached from unchanged code are safe, that the application has no other exposure — so this is a covered reading of the diff and never a security clearance.

Three verdicts, then. (PRESENT, BAD) for a quotable instance of the defect. (ABSENT, GOOD) when the added lines do carry untrusted input toward a sink and every such flow is neutralized. NO_REVIEW_OCCASION only when no untrusted value reaches a dangerous sink in the added lines at all, since that value claims the work had no subject here. The one further answer available to you is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, for a flow you can see whose neutralization the added lines do not settle.

THE STANDARD. When code added in this diff carries a value from outside the trust boundary into an operation where that value can change the operation's meaning, the value must be neutralized first — parameterized, escaped for the exact sink context, or validated against an allow-list/strict type — rather than concatenated or interpolated raw. Reason as an experienced security reviewer: a "source" is any externally-controlled value (e.g. a request param, header, body, uploaded filename, CLI arg, or a remote service's response); a "dangerous sink" is any place where raw text changes execution (e.g. a built query string, a shell command, an HTML/template render, a filesystem path, a redirect target, a deserializer/eval, or a constructed URL whose path/query interpolates the value — e.g. `"/auth/\(token)"` then `URL(string: base + path)`, where the fix is percent-encoding via the platform URL builder, not raw interpolation). These lists are illustrative, not exhaustive — recognize the shape in any language or stack, including sinks not named here.

GOOD looks like: the untrusted value reaches the sink bound as a parameter, run through a context-correct encoder, passed as an args array to exec, confined under a canonicalized base path, or rendered through auto-escaping left on. BAD looks like: the value is string-concatenated/interpolated straight into the sink with nothing in the quoted hunk neutralizing it.

PROCESS STANCE (look before you leap). Before abstaining either way, actually scan the added lines for a source-to-sink flow — don't skip it because the diff "looks routine." INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE is what you say after that scan finds a flow it cannot settle, never instead of it. But trace only what you can see: judge added/modified lines and their immediate in-diff context, and never assume code outside the diff sanitizes (or fails to sanitize) the value.

GROUNDING & ANTI-FABRICATION. A (PRESENT, BAD) finding must quote the exact added [L<n>] hunk where the source reaches the sink unneutralized, and name both the source and the sink end-to-end. If you cannot point to both on quoted added lines, it is not assertable: when no source-to-sink flow is visible at all, that is NO_REVIEW_OCCASION; when a flow IS visible and the added lines do not show whether it was neutralized, that is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. Never claim the code runs, compiles, is exploitable, or that a payload triggers; assert only the visible habit. Never invent a file, line, or clean bill you did not verify. If the diff is dominated by generated/vendored files, assess only the hand-written remainder.

SEVERITY (philosophy, not a lookup). This is a non-blocking, formative signal — a security habit to grow, never a merge gate, and it never exceeds MAJOR on this alone. Reserve the higher end for flows where raw input changes code/data execution (injection, traversal, RCE shapes); use the lower end for render/redirect/header-style flows; use the lightest nudge when the value is partly constrained but the context-correct escape is still missing. Use your judgment to place a given flow; identical hunks should land at the same level.

NON-BLOCKING & NO INTENT. Describe the observable behaviour (raw input flowing into a sink) and show the shape of the fix for the single most consequential flow — never impute intent or character.

DEFER BOUNDARY. This practice judges ONLY a taint-to-sink injection flow; a generic missing bounds/null/format check with no dangerous sink belongs to validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary, and a committed secret belongs to avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions — defer to the sibling rather than double-flag.
practices.whyItMatters: Gluing raw user input straight into a query, a shell command, or a page is how injection bugs are born, the kind that leak a database or run an attacker's code. Parameterizing or escaping it first is what keeps that door shut.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: User-supplied values reach the database through bound parameters and the page through proper escaping, never concatenated into a SQL string or dropped into HTML as-is.

practices.name: Avoid insecure defaults and over-broad permissions
practices.criteria:
DEFECT-DETECTOR DISCIPLINE: this practice hunts one specific defect — an added setting that ships an insecure default or widens an access boundary. What would be PRESENT for it is that setting, so (PRESENT, GOOD) is never available here: praising a security posture is not something a diff can support.

A clean result is a different claim, and the PROCESS below is exactly what earns it. This practice already requires you to walk a fixed list of sink classes across the added lines rather than glance at the diff, so a pass that found no offending setting is a COVERED search over a closed corpus, not an impression: (outcome occurrence=ABSENT, assessment=GOOD), the insecure default that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with evidence.exhaustiveSearch over scm.pull-request.diff, name the sink classes you walked in lookedFor, and state in boundary what you did NOT establish — that the existing configuration is sound, that unchanged settings are safe, that the system has no other exposure. This is a report on a search, never a security clearance.

Three verdicts, then. PRESENT, BAD for a quotable instance. (ABSENT, GOOD) when you walked every sink class over the added lines and none of them was touched insecurely. NO_REVIEW_OCCASION only when the added lines touch no setting of any sink class at all, since that value claims the work had no subject here. The one further answer available to you is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, for a candidate line you can see whose setting the evidence does not settle.

STANDARD (a sink-hunt, not a posture rating): code should start locked down and open only what it can justify. Your job is to HUNT the added (+) lines for a change that ships an insecure default or widens an access/exposure boundary with no stated reason. Judge the SETTING the change adopts, not the data flowing through it, and never as a blanket vulnerability scan. Frame the task as a search for specific sinks — do not read the top-level intent, conclude "looks secure", and stop.

PROCESS (look before you leap — SHOW YOUR WORK): you may NOT abstain, as NO_REVIEW_OCCASION or as INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, and you may not clear the change as (ABSENT, GOOD) either, on a shallow pass. The clean verdict is the strongest reason to do the walk properly: it reports that you covered the corpus, so an unwalked class makes it a false claim rather than merely an incomplete one. A security review walks a standard set of sink CLASSES; reason about each within the diff (these are classes to think in, not a closed value list — recognise the same shape on any stack):
  (1) transport / certificate / host verification toggled off;
  (2) cross-origin / CORS or permission scope widened (e.g. a credentialed response that reflects the request Origin back without an allowlist, or a bare wildcard on an authenticated route);
  (3) file / resource / object mode made world-readable/writable or over-broad;
  (4) an existing auth / authz guard removed or loosened;
  (5) secret or credential EXPOSURE — and trace dataflow here, do not pattern-match names: inspect EVERY logging, string-interpolation, persistence, and URL-building call in the added lines and ask what the interpolated value can hold at RUNTIME. A print/log of a request/response body, header, or any value derived from an auth/login/token/credential exchange is a leak even when the variable is not named "token" (e.g. a response body that carries the issued token);
  (6) a debug / verbose-error / permissive default shipped to a non-test surface.
Spotting one tightened setting (e.g. an ATS flag removed) does NOT discharge the hunt — finish every class. Do not depend on any precompute candidate list; an absent list is NEVER grounds for NA while such a line is visible. In your evidenceRationale, briefly state what you found for the credential-exposure class (5) before either abstention.

CLEAN (→ ABSENT, GOOD once you have walked every sink class): a setting correctly scoped/least-privilege/tightened; a widening carrying a quotable justification (an inline comment on the line, or a sentence in metadata.body, you can quote verbatim); or a change confined to an observably test/sample/fixture/local path. BAD (→ PRESENT): a concrete added instance of any class above, reasoned about by class — not by matching a fixed token.

SEVERITY (philosophy, not a lookup): non-blocking; never exceeds MAJOR on this alone. Reserve MAJOR for a meaningfully widened blast radius — disabled verification, credentialed origin-reflection or wildcard exposure, a removed/loosened auth guard, or exposed credential material — which stays MAJOR regardless of an internal-only or dev rationale. MINOR for lower-blast-radius misconfigs. If several issues appear, name the single most consequential and mention the rest in a clause; do not sum severities. INFO is unused here.

GROUNDING & ANTI-FABRICATION: quote the exact added [L<n>] line (or the removed/weakened guard line) and name the file for any finding; a NA resting on a justification must quote it. Never infer a setting from a filename or a count you cannot quote, and never claim to run/compile/test. If a candidate sink line is visible but the fact that would settle it is not, return INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE — never invent a file, line, or clean bill of health, and never file an unreadable sink under NO_REVIEW_OCCASION. Assess only the hand-written remainder of a generated/vendored-dominated diff.

NON-BLOCKING & NO INTENT: a security-hygiene habit to grow, not a merge gate. Describe the observable setting and point forward to the safer default (verification on; the exact origin named instead of `*`; the toggle behind a dev profile; the least-privilege mode; the guard restored or its reason recorded). Talk about the configuration, never the contributor.

DEFER BOUNDARY: this does not judge whether untrusted input is escaped/validated (a sibling owns that). It IS the terminal owner of exposed credential material — a hardcoded secret/token/API-key/password on a non-test path or in a URL/log. Report it here at MAJOR; never defer it elsewhere or NA it.
practices.whyItMatters: A default or permission that ships wider than it needs sits quietly until someone exploits it, and this kind of misconfiguration is among the most common security gaps there is. Starting locked down means you only open what you can justify.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A new endpoint or credential grants exactly the access it needs and no more, with scoped permissions and a specific allowed origin from an allowlist, not an origin reflected back from the request or a blanket wildcard, instead of a permissive default dropped in to make things work.

practices.name: Change dependencies deliberately

appliesWhen.absentSays: the change touches no dependency manifest or lockfile

practices.criteria:
## The standard
Judge whether this pull request edits its dependencies DELIBERATELY: when the manifest (where a human declares a dependency and its version) changes, the lockfile (the pinned resolution) moves with it, and a notable new dependency or version bump carries a one-line reason a reviewer can read. This is a supply-chain workflow habit (OWASP A06, reproducible builds) about how a dependency edit is justified and kept coherent — never a claim about the dependency's own correctness, its CVEs, or whether the chosen version is the "right" one.

## Good vs. bad (open examples — reason about the rest)
GOOD: a new direct runtime dependency arrives with a sentence on what it is for (in the manifest context, the PR title/body, or a commit subject) and the lockfile updates in the same change; a routine transitive resolution refresh that is internally consistent. BAD: a manifest adds or major-bumps a runtime dependency but the lockfile that exists for that ecosystem was left untouched (the build no longer resolves reproducibly from the manifest as written); a notable add lands as an unexplained pin with no quotable why; a version pin is loosened or dropped so a future build could silently resolve something else. Use your judgment as an experienced reviewer for manifests, lockfiles, and ecosystems not named here — the principle (coherence + a traceable reason for notable changes), not a fixed file list, decides. A patch/minor bump or a transitive-only delta needs no prose, and a large generated lockfile delta is normal EVIDENCE of coherence, not a problem.

## Presence, assessment, severity (as principles)
Emit a finding only when a real dependency surface (manifest or lockfile) is in the changed set and the deciding hunk is quotable; otherwise NO_REVIEW_OCCASION. Coherent-and-explained is PRESENT, GOOD. Incoherence (manifest and lockfile out of step on something that ships) is the most serious case here; an unexplained-but-coherent notable pin is a milder, formative nudge; a loosened/dropped pin always deserves at least a gentle flag. Scale severity to how much reproducibility is actually at risk, and never exceed MAJOR on dependency deliberateness alone — this is a non-blocking habit to grow, not a merge gate. Describe the observable edit; never impute intent or character. Identical hunks must yield identical assessments.

## Grounding, boundaries, look-before-you-leap
Every claim cites observable evidence: quote the manifest line, the matching or missing lockfile span, and the explaining sentence/commit-subject verbatim. Before calling a manifest edit orphaned, confirm a lockfile for that ecosystem actually exists and was left out — if none exists in the repo, the manifest is coherent by absence. To call a notable change unexplained you must actually have read the diff, the title, the body and the commit subjects; when one of those surfaces was not materialized for you, your search was incomplete, so return INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE rather than NO_REVIEW_OCCASION, which would claim no dependency change was here. Never invent a file, a reason, a CVE, or a clean bill you did not verify. You see subjects, the file-spread table, and the quoted hunks, not per-commit patches — judge from what is quotable. Defer artifact-hygiene and review-size concerns about generated churn to its sibling practice; assess only deliberateness.
practices.whyItMatters: Every dependency you add is code you now trust and have to keep patched, and many malicious packages slip in disguised as a real name a letter or two off. A one-line note on why a package is there, plus a lockfile that moves with the manifest, lets a reviewer sanity-check the addition and keeps the build reproducible.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A new package arrives with a sentence on what it is for, and the lockfile is updated in the same change as the manifest so the build still resolves the same way.

groups.name: Recording decisions and documenting changes
groups.description: Capture the why. Record the evidenceRationale behind significant design decisions, and document changes to public APIs and shared behaviour, so the people who maintain or build on the code later can understand it.

practices.name: Record significant decisions and the evidenceRationale
practices.criteria:
## The standard
This practice judges ONE thing: when this PR makes an architecturally SIGNIFICANT decision, is the WHY recorded somewhere a future maintainer can find it — a written rationale (constraint, trade-off, or alternative rejected) — rather than left for them to reverse-engineer from the code? Significance is the kind of choice a senior reviewer would expect a sentence about: a new dependency or framework, a schema/data-model change, a public-contract or wire-API change, a new cross-cutting mechanism the rest of the app plugs into (a shared aspect/interceptor/event bus, a base class many types extend), or an auth/security mechanism. These are illustrative, not a closed list — use your judgment about what is genuinely structural versus routine. Routine work (tests, formatting, docs, renames without contract change, a version bump of an already-present dependency, a tuned constant/threshold on an internal symbol) carries no architectural decision: emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION.

Two stages, in order: (1) decide whether the hand-written diff contains a significant decision; (2) ONLY if it does, check whether its rationale is recorded in the title, body, a commit subject, or a linked ADR/design-doc. When the change references a design doc or ADR that lives in the team wiki, that document's body may be materialized for you as a `.md` file under `inputs/context/outline/` — read it before concluding the why is absent. When it names a specific document that was NOT materialized for you, the rationale may well be recorded there: that is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, never a finding against prose you were never shown. A rationale clause counts whether it sits in prose or inside a bullet/checklist item ("chose X because Y", "an event queue so a slow consumer can't block checkout", "to avoid Z") — scan the whole body. Restating WHAT changed, an empty or template body, or a bare "added dependency X" does not record a why.

## Good vs bad
GOOD (PRESENT): a significant decision is present and its evidenceRationale is written down, so the intent survives without re-reading the code. BAD: a significant decision ships with no recorded why anywhere in the body, the commit subjects, or a linked ADR.

## Severity philosophy
Non-blocking; never exceed MAJOR on rationale alone. A single contained unexplained decision (one new dependency, one isolated column, one app-internal class) is a light MINOR nudge. Reserve MAJOR for the genuinely consequential: an unexplained auth/security mechanism, a persistence/public-API/wire-contract change, a real cross-cutting mechanism others build on, or several significant decisions co-occurring unexplained. When unsure, prefer the lower severity.

## Grounding and stance
Ground every PRESENT/BAD finding in observable evidence: quote the exact added [L<n>] line(s) establishing significance, and for a GOOD finding also quote the verbatim rationale sentence/subject/reference. If the diff is empty there is nothing to scan — emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION. If the diff is unreadable, the change still made whatever decisions it made and you could not read them — emit INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE; never treat a missing diff as routine or significant. Per-commit patches are not in your context — judge significance from the diff and subjects, never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot see. Detect significance from hand-written hunks only; a dependency echoed solely in a lockfile (no manifest edit) is not an independent decision, but a hand-authored migration changeset is. Never invent a rationale the author did not write, never infer the why from the code itself, and never assert the dependency/schema/endpoint is wrong — judge only whether the WHY is recorded. Describe the observable behaviour; never impute intent or character. When the rationale lives in a linked wiki document rather than the PR body, cite that document's `inputs/context/outline/...` file path together with the quoted or closely paraphrased rationale sentence — a bare URL to the doc is not itself evidence the why was recorded.

## Defer boundary
The overall adequacy of the PR description (a clear title + a why for the change as a whole) belongs to describe-what-and-why; here judge only whether THAT significant decision's rationale is recorded, so the two never double-flag.
practices.whyItMatters: When you pick one design over another, the evidenceRationale is the first thing to fade. A maintainer who cannot find why you chose it will either undo a good decision or be too afraid to touch it, and both cost the team later.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A meaningful design choice arrives with its evidenceRationale written down, in the description or a short architecture decision record (ADR), such as 'chose an event queue over direct calls so a slow consumer cannot block checkout', not just the code that does it.

practices.name: Document public API and behaviour changes
practices.criteria:
STANDARD. This practice judges one habit: when a change alters a PUBLIC/SHARED surface — something a SEPARATE consumer depends on and compiles or integrates against (a library/framework's exported symbols, a published package's API, a documented HTTP/RPC contract, a persisted or wire schema, an error/response shape callers branch on, a config default a consumer sets) — does that change carry, in the SAME diff or in metadata.body, documentation that tells consumers what moved? Good means the renamed parameter, new endpoint, changed response field, or breaking removal lands with its doc-comment, changelog line, or a body sentence naming the consumer-facing effect, so a downstream caller hears it from the change itself. Bad means a real exported-surface change ships with nothing a consumer could read to adapt.

GATE FIRST. A single application target with no library product has no public API: internal types, private signatures, local refactors, and app-only fields are NOT public surfaces — emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION. Use your judgment as an experienced reviewer to decide whether a changed symbol is actually exported and consumer-facing, rather than matching keywords; when a changed symbol is plainly internal, NO_REVIEW_OCCASION is right; when the evidence genuinely cannot settle whether the one symbol this practice turns on crosses a module/service boundary, answer INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE rather than resolving the doubt into either a false finding or a claim that no public surface was here. Generated/vendored artifacts (codegen specs, *.gen.*, lockfiles, route trees, dist) count as neither a surface to flag nor as documentation — assess only the hand-written remainder.

ASSESSMENT & SEVERITY (principles, not a lookup table). Non-blocking and never exceeds MAJOR — this is a formative habit, not a merge gate. Scale severity to consumer impact: a breaking change (removed/renamed symbol, route, or field; a narrowed type; a changed default) shipping with no documentation anywhere is the most serious because callers break without a migration note (up to MAJOR); a new additive surface with no documentation is gentler because nothing breaks but consumers cannot discover it; documentation that exists yet never names the specific changed parameter/field is the gentlest nudge. When several surfaces change, grade by the least-documented one. Equivalent situations should land at equivalent severity.

GROUNDING. Cite the observable surface change and either quote the documenting text or, before concluding it is undocumented, look in all the places a consumer would: a doc-comment on or above the surface, a changelog/docs addition, metadata.body, and — when the change references a wiki doc — that document's body materialized as a `.md` file under `inputs/context/outline/`. When the change points at a specific document that was not materialized for you, the documentation consumers need may live there: that is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, not an undocumented surface. If no public-surface change is observable in the provided diff and body, return NO_REVIEW_OCCASION — never invent a symbol, an export marker, a changelog, or a clean bill you did not see. Describe only the documentation habit on the observable artifact; never assert compile/runtime correctness of the surface and never impute the author's intent or care. When a linked wiki document supplies that documentation, cite its `inputs/context/outline/...` file path together with the quoted or closely paraphrased sentence relied on — a bare URL is not evidence that the doc actually says it.

DEFER. You judge only whether the public-surface change is documented for consumers — not the PR's general what/why narrative (describe-what-and-why) nor whether a design decision's rationale is recorded (records-significant-decisions-with-rationale). A thin body or unjustified choice is not a finding here; a finding requires an actual quotable public-surface change.
practices.whyItMatters: People outside your code depend on what you export. Change a public function or endpoint without a note and they find out at runtime, in their own project, with no warning, and they trust your library a little less each time.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A renamed parameter or a changed response shape lands with its reference docs and a changelog line updated in the same change, so the people building on your API hear about it from you, not from a broken build.

practices.name: Keep linked wiki docs consistent with the change
practices.criteria:
## The standard
This practice judges ONE thing: when this PR changes a documented behaviour — a config default, a public API or wire contract, a CLI flag, an error/return code, an operational step — AND the team wiki has a document describing that same behaviour, does the linked document still agree with the code after the change, or has the diff silently left the doc contradicting reality? A wiki document is available to you ONLY when the PR (its body, or a linked issue) references it: that document's body is materialized for you as a `.md` file under `inputs/context/outline/`. Read that file before concluding. If the PR references no such document, or the diff does not touch anything the materialized document describes, there is nothing to reconcile — emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION. If the PR does reference a specific document that a reader would expect to describe the behaviour this diff changes, and that document was not materialized for you, you cannot tell whether it now contradicts the code — that is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. The presence or absence of a wiki link is NEVER itself the finding; a change with no relevant doc is simply not applicable, not a weakness.

Two stages, in order: (1) from the hand-written diff, identify a concrete behaviour/contract/config the change alters; (2) ONLY if a materialized doc describes that same thing, check whether the doc now asserts something the code contradicts — an old default, a removed flag, a renamed field, a changed status code, a superseded step. A genuine contradiction between a specific doc passage and a specific diff hunk is the signal — not staleness in the abstract, and not "the code changed so the doc is probably old."

## Good vs bad
GOOD (PRESENT): the diff changes something the linked doc describes AND the same PR updates that doc (or the doc already reflects the new behaviour), so code and doc do not contradict. BAD: the diff changes a documented behaviour and the linked doc still asserts the old behaviour, leaving a reader who trusts the wiki misled.

## Severity philosophy
Non-blocking; never exceed MAJOR. A contradiction on a minor or internal-facing detail is a MINOR nudge to update the doc. Reserve MAJOR for a contradiction a consumer would act on wrongly: a wrong documented default/limit, a removed-but-still-documented API or flag, a changed auth/security or data-handling step. When unsure, prefer the lower severity — the aim is to keep the wiki trustworthy, not to gate the merge.

## Grounding and stance
Ground every BAD finding in BOTH sides of the contradiction: quote the exact added/removed [L<n>] diff line that changes the behaviour AND quote the verbatim sentence from the materialized `.md` doc that still asserts the old behaviour. If you cannot point to a specific doc passage the diff makes false, do not raise the finding — never infer a contradiction you cannot cite, and never fabricate a doc quote. Ground the doc side of the contradiction with the document's `inputs/context/outline/...` file path alongside the quoted sentence — a bare URL from the PR body is not evidence, since only the materialized text confirms what the doc actually says. If the PR references no doc at all, the diff is empty, or the change does not intersect any documented subject, emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION; if the diff is unreadable, emit INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE instead. This practice is disjoint from documents-public-api-and-behaviour-changes (which asks whether a change was documented AT ALL, in any surface) and from records-significant-decisions-with-rationale (which asks whether the WHY is recorded): here the question is narrowly whether a specific linked wiki doc now CONTRADICTS the code.
practices.whyItMatters: A wiki that contradicts the code is worse than no wiki: teammates act on documented behaviour that no longer holds, and the drift compounds silently until someone is burned by it.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When a change alters something the team's design or reference doc describes, the same PR brings the doc along, so the wiki keeps telling the truth about the system.

practices.name: Point the issue to the context it depends on
practices.criteria:
## The standard
This practice judges ONE thing: when an issue clearly DEPENDS on prior context an implementer would need — an existing design, a decision record, a spec, a runbook, a data model — to act on it correctly, does the issue point them to that context (a link to the relevant wiki document) instead of assuming the reader already carries it? Most issues are self-contained: a clear bug report, a small well-described change, a question. Those need no external context — emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION. The signal is judged from the issue's OWN text: does it lean on decisions or designs made elsewhere ("per our architecture", "following the agreed rollout plan", "as decided for the billing redesign", "must match the data model") such that someone picking it up cold could not proceed correctly without finding that source? When a referenced wiki document is materialized for you under `inputs/context/outline/`, read it to judge whether it is actually the relevant context. When the issue links a specific document that was NOT materialized for you, you cannot tell whether it carries the context the issue leans on — that is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, neither credit nor a finding. A link COUNT is never the signal, and adding a link to an unrelated doc is not credit.

## Good vs bad
GOOD (PRESENT): an issue that genuinely rests on prior design/decision/spec context links the specific document that carries it, so an implementer can proceed without hunting or guessing. BAD: an issue plainly leans on context made elsewhere ("as we decided…", "per the design") but leaves the reader no pointer to it, so they must reconstruct or reverse-engineer the intent.

## Severity philosophy
Non-blocking; never exceed MAJOR. A mild lean on unstated context is a MINOR nudge to link the source. Reserve MAJOR only when the missing context is load-bearing enough that an implementer would likely build the wrong thing without it. When unsure, prefer the lower severity, and prefer NO_REVIEW_OCCASION whenever the issue reads as self-contained.

## Grounding and stance
Ground every BAD finding by quoting the exact phrase in the issue that appeals to external context ("as decided…", "per the design", "must match…") and stating what context an implementer would need but is not pointed to. Do not infer a hidden dependency the text does not express, and never penalize a self-contained issue for lacking links. If the issue is self-contained, or the referenced document is materialized and is in fact the relevant context, emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION (self-contained) or GOOD (linked appropriately). When judging whether a linked document is the relevant context, cite its materialized `inputs/context/outline/...` file path and quote or closely paraphrase the passage that shows it is relevant — a bare link in the issue text is not evidence on its own. This is disjoint from issue-states-an-actionable-problem (which asks whether the issue is actionable on its own terms): here the question is narrowly whether an issue that DEPENDS on external design/decision context actually points to it.
practices.whyItMatters: An issue that silently depends on decisions made elsewhere forces every implementer to re-discover the context — or, worse, to guess it and build the wrong thing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When work depends on an existing design or decision, the issue links the document that holds it, so whoever picks it up starts with the evidenceRationale already in hand.

practices.name: Say what else you considered
practices.criteria:
## The standard
Judge whether a published decision record says what else was seriously considered and why those options lost. A record that states only the chosen option records an outcome; what a later reader needs is the evidenceRationale, because that is the only part that tells them whether the decision still holds once a constraint changes.

## What to read
`inputs/context/document.md` — the document's own body. Judge the text in front of you and nothing else.

## When this applies
Only when the document is recognisably a decision record: it names a single decision and takes a position on it. Signals include a title or heading naming a decision, a status line (proposed / accepted / superseded), or a section headed with words like decision, context, consequences, options, alternatives, trade-offs. A design overview, a runbook, a how-to guide, a meeting note, an index page or a specification that decides nothing is NO_REVIEW_OCCASION — stay silent rather than asking it to be a decision record.

## Present
The document names at least one alternative that was genuinely on the table and says why it was not chosen — a constraint it failed, a cost it carried, a trade-off the team was unwilling to make. The reason must be about that alternative specifically. Quote the span naming the alternative and the span giving the reason.

## Absent
The document states a decision and its rationale but names no alternative at all; or it lists alternatives with no reason any of them lost (a bare bullet list of technology names); or the only reason given restates the chosen option's merits, which says nothing about why the others were worse. A section headed 'Alternatives considered' that is empty, or contains only 'none', counts as absent unless the document explains why there was genuinely no other option. Two cases are not absence: a record that defers its options discussion to another document you were not given, and a body that visibly breaks off before any options section. Both are INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE — a decision record is in front of you and the text you have does not settle it.

## Do not
Do not judge whether the decision was correct, whether the rejected alternatives deserved to be rejected, or whether the document is still up to date — none of that is observable here. Do not demand a specific template or heading name; a document that gives the evidenceRationale in prose satisfies this as fully as one with a headed section.
practices.whyItMatters: A decision record that names only the winner tells the next person what was done, not what it cost. When a constraint later changes — a library is deprecated, the traffic grows, the team shrinks — the first question is always "what else did we look at, and does that reason still hold?". If the alternatives were never written down, that question can only be answered by redoing the whole investigation, and usually it is not answered at all: the decision quietly becomes something nobody feels able to revisit.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A record that names the two or three options that were genuinely in play and gives each one a sentence saying what ruled it out — the constraint it failed, the cost it carried, the thing the team was not willing to trade. Written for someone who arrives a year later with a changed constraint, so they can tell in a minute whether the decision still stands.

groups.name: Disciplined delivery and version control
groups.description: Keep your delivery clean. Make each commit one self-contained change, leave generated and build files out of the diff, and branch from the shared integration branch so your work stands on its own.

practices.name: Keep each commit to one logical change
practices.criteria:
## The standard
Judge one thing: whether the PR's commits are SPLIT so each one captures a single logical change, rather than one commit tangling unrelated kinds of work into a bundle a reviewer cannot follow, revert, or cherry-pick on its own. This is a workflow habit about how the history is partitioned — describe the observable split, never impute intent or character, and never frame it as a code-defect claim.

## What good vs bad looks like
GOOD: each commit reads as one cohesive logical unit — e.g. a fix and the test that covers it together, or a single change described in two clauses about the same step ("parse the header and validate it"). Multiple cohesive feature commits in one PR is fine here. BAD: a subject that plainly conjoins distinct concerns (e.g. a behavioural fix bundled with an unrelated reformat/lint sweep, a rename-sweep, a merge-conflict resolution, or a dependency bump), or a series that obviously braids process/chore work through behavioural work. Use your judgment as an experienced reviewer about what counts as "unrelated" — no fixed word list; a conjunction joining clauses about the SAME change is not a tangle.

## Presence / assessment / severity
PRESENT, GOOD when the commits read as cohesive logical units. assessment=BAD when the split itself is wrong. Severity is non-blocking and never exceeds MAJOR on commit atomicity alone: lean MINOR when a single commit bundles unrelated work (splitting it would isolate each concern), and MAJOR only when the history broadly tangles so a reviewer cannot reason about or revert one concern at a time. This is a formative habit to grow, not a merge gate.

## Grounding and honest context boundaries
Your evidence is inputs/context/commits.json — one entry per commit, oldest authored first, each with its `subject`, its `body` when the message had one, and its `additions`, `deletions` and `changedFiles` — plus the per-file changed-line spread of the whole change; per-commit patches are NOT in your context, so you cannot see which files belong to which commit — judge conservatively from subjects, bodies, per-commit size and overall spread, and never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot observe. Quote the deciding subject(s) for any BAD finding. Every claim must cite an observable subject; if you cannot quote a subject that conjoins or braids unrelated concerns, treat the history as cohesive (PRESENT, GOOD) — never invent a tangle the subjects do not state. Emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION when there was no split to judge — only a single non-merge commit, or every entry is an automatic merge commit (`parentCount` of 2 or more, or a "Merge ..." subject) — and name which. When `truncated` is true the file holds the first 200 commits only: judge what you can read and say the list was cut. Do NOT attach a file/diff-line location to this finding — its evidence is the subject text, not a diff line.

## Defer boundary
Defer overall PR size and file spread to scope-one-reviewable-change, and subject wording/legibility to commit-subjects-explain-each-change — a vague-but-cohesive subject, or a large-but-cohesive change, is a strength here, not a tangle.
practices.whyItMatters: A commit that mixes an unrelated refactor in with a bug fix cannot be cleanly reverted or cherry-picked, so you are stuck taking the bad with the good. One logical change per commit keeps your history a tool you can act on instead of a tangle.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Separate commits for separate ideas, such as 'Fix off-by-one in pagination' in one and 'Rename helper for clarity' in another, so each can be reviewed, reverted, or backported on its own.

practices.name: Keep generated and build files out of the diff
practices.criteria:
## The standard
This practice judges ONE thing: does the change keep machine-emitted output and committed cruft OUT of the diff, so a reviewer reads only what a human hand-wrote? Treat it as a repository-hygiene habit about *what gets committed* — never as a code-defect claim about the file's contents.

Judge from the file PATHS in the diff (the per-file table and the per-file headers). You MAY open the patch to confirm a flagged path is machine-emitted when the path alone is ambiguous — e.g. a "DO NOT EDIT"/"@generated"/"auto-generated" banner, or a minified single-line bundle — but the evidence is the path plus that confirming line, not a line-by-line review of the file's contents.

## What good vs bad looks like
GOOD: every changed path is something a person authored or intended — source, tests, docs, config you wrote, or a lockfile that moves in step with its manifest in the same diff. Use your judgment as an experienced reviewer: a build-output directory, an editor/OS cruft file, a coverage dump, a vendored/cached blob, or a tracked generated file someone hand-edited instead of regenerating are all signs that machine noise is being reviewed as if it were source. These are open examples, not a closed list — recognise the underlying shape (a location or banner that says "a tool wrote this") across any stack or language.

A repo may DELIBERATELY version-control some generated sources (a committed OpenAPI spec, a generated client, an ERD, a routeTree). When such a tracked artifact moves IN STEP with the hand-written change that drives its regeneration, that is intended, regeneration-consistent movement — do not flag it. Flag only output that is not meant to be tracked, or a tracked generated file left hand-edited/stale relative to its source.

## Presence, assessment, severity (as principles)
PRESENT when the diff carries quotable file paths whose committed-hygiene you can read; otherwise NO_REVIEW_OCCASION. Also return NO_REVIEW_OCCASION when machine-emitted paths are essentially the whole diff — a pure regeneration/build commit has no hand-authored remainder whose hygiene this practice can meaningfully judge; do not blanket-grade an intentional regeneration as BAD.

GOOD when no changed path is machine-emitted output or cruft. BAD when at least one is. Severity is non-blocking and never exceeds MAJOR on this practice alone: a lone stray artifact is minor; a committed build-output directory, several leaked artifacts, or a hand-edited generated file that should have been regenerated weighs toward MAJOR. Use reviewer judgment on where in that band a case sits; identical situations should land identically.

## Grounding and stance
Every BAD finding must quote each offending path verbatim and, for a generated-file flag, quote the confirming banner or name the tracked artifact. If you cannot quote an offending path, there is nothing to flag — do not invent one, and never assert compile/build/runtime behaviour from a path.
