When the one path this practice turns on is genuinely ambiguous — the path, any banner, and the patch together cannot tell you whether it is machine-emitted, or whether a tracked generated artifact moved in step with the source that drives it — emit INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE rather than letting that doubt pass as a clean bill. Describe the observable fact (this path is machine-emitted) and the next step (gitignore it and drop it, or regenerate from source); never impute intent or character. This is a habit to grow, not a merge gate.

## Defer boundary
Whether a dependency change was deliberate or justified belongs to the sibling changes-dependencies-deliberately, not here — a lockfile moving in step with its manifest is its concern, not yours; you flag a lockfile only when it is hand-edited out of step with any manifest in the diff.
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer catches the most problems in the hand-written lines they can read closely, and a committed build output or editor config buries that source under machine noise nobody reviews. Leaving generated files out keeps the diff to the change a person can actually check, and spares everyone the odd conflict in a file no human wrote.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The diff holds only the source you hand-wrote, with build outputs, logs, and editor files kept out through .gitignore. If the repo deliberately tracks a generated file, such as a committed API spec or client, that is fine as long as it was regenerated and moves in step with the source change that drives it, not hand-edited.

groups.name: Tracking and planning the work
groups.description: Plan and track the work so a maintainer can route it and watch it progress. Split genuinely large issues into trackable sub-tasks, and triage each one with the labels, assignee, or milestone that tells the team where it belongs.

practices.name: Break large work into trackable subtasks
practices.criteria:
Judge ONE thing: when an issue describes genuinely LARGE or multi-part work, is that work broken into explicit, trackable sub-units a maintainer can watch reach done — rather than left as a single monolithic ask? Trackable means the parts are individually checkable or addressable: a task list of checkboxes that name work to do, a tracked sub-issue tree, or enumerated child/tracking issues. Reason like a senior reviewer scanning a backlog: a big ask written as one undivided block is either 0% or 100% done with no visible progress; a decomposed one lets pieces be picked up in parallel and tracked to done.

GOOD looks like: a large issue split into named sub-steps (e.g. "design the schema", "add the endpoint", "wire up the UI") as a checklist, or as linked child issues the body frames as parts. BAD looks like: a clearly large, multi-deliverable ask carrying no breakdown of any kind — e.g. an epic/tracking-style issue with nothing tracked under it, or a body that enumerates several independent deliverables as prose with no way to track each.

Use your judgment on what counts as LARGE. The signal is two or more SEPARABLE deliverables that could ship or be assigned independently, or an explicit epic/initiative/meta/tracking framing the author themselves chose. Sequential steps of ONE cohesive flow described as a journey are a single deliverable, not several parts. When the issue text genuinely cannot settle whether its spans are one journey or several separable deliverables, and no trackable breakdown exists on any surface, that is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE — do not resolve the doubt into silence. A focused single-concern issue (one feature, one bug) is not large: it neither needs nor is penalised for lacking a checklist.

Presence/assessment/severity as principles, not a lookup table: emit PRESENT, GOOD only when the work is genuinely large AND a trackable breakdown is quotable. When the work is not large enough to need a breakdown, emit NO_REVIEW_OCCASION (stay silent) — never manufacture a strength from the mere absence of largeness, and never make the single-concern scope judgment that belongs to issue-scoped-to-single-concern. Emit assessment=BAD only when the work is clearly large AND no trackable breakdown exists on any surface. Scale severity to the gap, never above MAJOR (this is a non-blocking workflow habit, not a merge gate): heaviest when an explicitly epic/tracking-framed issue has nothing to track; lighter when only a couple of parts go untracked. Identical evidence should yield the same call.

GROUNDING: every "large" claim and every "no breakdown" claim must quote the exact span — a label name, body text, the sub_issues rollup figure, or a comment. Before concluding a breakdown is absent, actually scan ALL of: body, the sub_issues_total/sub_issues_completed rollup, and comments — look before you leap. An element you cannot quote is counted absent; never invent largeness from title length or tone, and never fabricate a breakdown you did not see. Your context is the ISSUE only — title, body, labels, the metadata rollup, and comments; there is NO diff or code, so never assert technical feasibility, hour-estimates, or design correctness, and never grade the reporter as a person. Describe observable artifact state only.

DEFER boundary: this practice asks only whether large work is DECOMPOSED. Whether the work SHOULD have been one concern, and whether acceptance-criteria / Definition-of-Done conditions are present, are owned by sibling practices — treat a multi-part ask as legitimately large work needing a breakdown, and do not re-flag a verification checklist as if it were a work-breakdown unless it also names concrete implementation sub-steps.

NO_REVIEW_OCCASION when the issue is a pure question, support request, or open discussion with no concrete deliverable; when the body is empty, title-only, or an unmodified template (nothing quotable); or when it is a small single-concern deliverable so the breakdown question does not arise.
practices.whyItMatters: A big ask written as one wall of text is either 0% or 100% done, with no way to see progress or split the load. Breaking it into checkable steps turns a daunting job into pieces people can pick up and finish one at a time.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A genuinely large issue split into a task list or linked sub-issues, such as 'design the schema', 'add the endpoint', and 'wire up the UI', so progress is visible and pieces can be worked in parallel.

practices.name: Classify issues for triage
practices.criteria:
## The standard
Judge whether a substantive issue carries filterable classification metadata that helps maintainers find and group it during triage. A native issue type or a meaningful category label satisfies the standard. Assess only what is present, not whether the chosen type, label, assignee, or milestone is correct.

## What good vs bad looks like
GOOD: a native issue type or a label that identifies an area, component, priority, or severity. Stay vocabulary-agnostic: do not require a particular taxonomy, prefix, color, or provider. Social and lifecycle labels such as "good first issue", "help wanted", "duplicate", "wontfix", or "stale" do not classify the work by themselves. An assignee or milestone adds useful context but does not classify the work.
BAD: a substantive issue has no native type or meaningful category label.

## Presence, assessment, and severity
This is a non-blocking discoverability practice and never exceeds MINOR. Return PRESENT/GOOD when a native type or meaningful category label is present. Return INFO when classification is absent but an assignee or milestone makes the issue easier to find in an ownership or planning view. Return MINOR when a substantive issue has none of these signals. Identical metadata yields identical assessment.

Return NO_REVIEW_OCCASION for a pure question, support request, or open discussion with no concrete unit of work. If the issue is substantive but the metadata is unavailable rather than observably empty, return INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. An empty body does not by itself excuse an observably unclassified unit of work.

## Grounding and boundaries
Quote the exact native type or label used as evidence and state whether an assignee and milestone are present. Never invent metadata, assess its correctness, infer intent, or judge whether the work is worth doing. Defer problem framing, scope, and definition of done to the sibling issue practices.
practices.whyItMatters: Unclassified work is harder to find and group during triage, so it is more likely to be overlooked or repeatedly re-read.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A substantive issue has a native issue type or a meaningful category label that lets maintainers find related work without opening every issue.

practices.name: Confirm the outcome before closing the issue
practices.criteria:
## The standard
When an issue is CLOSED as done, judge whether its own stated definition-of-done was actually confirmed before the close — every checkable acceptance item ticked and every tracked sub-issue finished — versus the issue being closed with a done-condition still visibly open. Frame this strictly as a lifecycle habit ("confirm the outcome before you close"), NEVER as a claim that the work itself is wrong or incomplete: an empty checkbox may simply never have been ticked while the work was genuinely done, or the remainder may be tracked elsewhere.

You read only the issue text in your context — title, body, labels, state, state_reason, the sub-issue rollup (completed of total), closed_at, and comment bodies. There is no diff or code here. Never assert compile/runtime/correctness behaviour, and never read a missing or absent rollup as zero.

## What good vs needs-work looks like
GOOD: closed as done with every checkable item ticked and every tracked sub-issue completed — "closed" honestly means done. NEEDS-WORK: closed as done while a stated done-item is still open, e.g. an unchecked acceptance/Definition-of-Done line, or a sub-issue rollup short of complete, with nothing at close naming where that remainder went.

## Presence, assessment, severity (principles)
PRESENT only when the issue is genuinely CLOSED *as done* AND it actually stated a checkable outcome you can quote (a task-list, an acceptance/DoD block, a Given-When-Then, or a non-zero sub-issue rollup). If the issue isn't closed, was closed as not-planned / wontfix / duplicate / superseded / deferred (an unmet checklist is the *expected* state for deliberately-abandoned work), or stated no checkable outcome at all, return NO_REVIEW_OCCASION and stay silent. Read the disposition from the observable fact — prefer an explicit state_reason, else an explicit closing-comment/body signal; a bare close with no not-planned signal defaults to done. Do not invent a state_reason the artifact never carried.

Assessment is GOOD when the stated outcome was confirmed, BAD when a stated done-item was left open at close. Severity is a judgment, not a lookup: an unconfirmed *acceptance/DoD* condition is the heavier lapse; an open *sub-issue rollup* alone is lighter. Crucially, LOOK BEFORE YOU CONCLUDE — scan every closing comment and the body for a disposition that explains the remainder (e.g. "deferred to #123", "covered by !45", "done, forgot to tick"). If the disposition was named at close, the habit was largely honoured, so keep severity low; reserve the higher band for an open done-item with *nothing anywhere* accounting for it. This practice is non-blocking and never exceeds MAJOR on outcome-confirmation alone; identical inputs yield identical severity.

## Grounding and stance
Every claim cites an exact quoted span — the unchecked line, the "N of M" rollup, the state/state_reason value. A BAD finding must quote the deciding span; an abstention names what you scanned (body, comments, rollup, state). If the issue is closed as done and stated a checkable outcome, but the deciding fact isn't observable — an absent rollup, a comment set you could not read — return INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE; NO_REVIEW_OCCASION belongs to the scope rules above, not to evidence you could not read. Never fabricate a checklist, a clean bill, or a disposition.

Describe only observable state ("closed as done with '<quoted line>' still unchecked"), never a charge against the closer ("you left it unfinished"). The feed-forward lesson is the habit: before closing, tick the items, close the child issues, or leave a comment naming what's deferred and filing a follow-up.

## Defer boundary
Whether a *new/open* issue defines a checkable outcome belongs to the sibling issue-has-checkable-outcome; this practice owns only the single at-close question of whether a stated outcome was confirmed.
practices.whyItMatters: Closing an issue tells the whole team it is handled. Closing it with a checklist item still unticked or sub-issues still open drops that work quietly, and someone hits the gap later expecting it to be done.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Before closing, every acceptance item is checked and every tracked sub-issue is finished, or a comment says plainly what is being dropped and why, so 'closed' honestly means done.

groups.name: Communicating in the open
groups.description: How you talk to teammates in shared channels: ask questions someone can actually answer, give answers people can act on, and keep others informed about where the work stands and what is blocking it. This is about the clarity of the exchange, not the correctness of the code being discussed.

practices.name: Ask questions a teammate can answer
practices.criteria:
## The standard
Judge whether a question raised in this conversation gives a teammate enough to answer it in a single reply, rather than forcing a round of clarifying questions first. A well-formed ask names the concrete goal, what was already tried, and what actually happened or is blocking; a bare "it doesn't work" or "how do I do this?" with no context makes the responder guess. Judge only the observable habit of how the question is posed, never whether the underlying problem is real, hard, or worth solving.

## Good vs. bad
GOOD (PRESENT, GOOD): a question a knowledgeable teammate could answer from the message alone because it states the objective and the specific point of confusion or the exact behaviour seen. BAD: a question so thin on context that answering it requires asking the author to explain what they mean, what they tried, or what they expected. Use judgment about how much context the question genuinely needs; a quick clarification among people sharing obvious context is not a defect.

## Severity philosophy (non-blocking)
This is a formative habit, never a gate. Scale severity to how much a responder must extract before they can help: a light nudge when a little more detail would sharpen the ask; heavier when the question as written cannot be answered without a full exchange of clarifications first. It never exceeds MAJOR on question phrasing alone. Describe the observable gap, never impute laziness or intent.

## Grounding and abstention
Quote the exact turn you assessed. Return NO_REVIEW_OCCASION when the turn is not actually a question (a statement, an acknowledgement, social chat), when the shared context plainly supplies what an outside reader would think is missing, or when there is no settled conversation to read. When a question IS asked but the thread you were given begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether what it leans on was supplied in a turn you never saw, return INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. Never invent missing context or grade an exchange you cannot quote.
practices.whyItMatters: A vague question forces the person helping you to stop and ask what you actually mean before they can even start, turning a one-message answer into a slow exchange. A question that carries its own context gets answered on the first reply.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A question that says what you are trying to do, what you already tried, and exactly where it broke, so a teammate can answer it in a single reply without asking you anything first.

practices.name: Give answers people can act on
practices.criteria:
## The standard
Judge whether a reply to someone's question actually moves them forward, rather than leaving them where they started. A useful answer either resolves the question directly or names a concrete next step the asker can take; a reply that only restates the problem, points vaguely at "the docs", or answers a different question does not. Judge only the observable helpfulness of the reply as written, never whether the technical content is ultimately correct.

## Good vs. bad
GOOD (PRESENT, GOOD): a reply the asker could act on immediately because it gives the answer, the specific place to look, or the exact next step. BAD: a reply to a genuine question that leaves the asker still stuck, because it is too vague to act on or sidesteps what was asked. A short answer can be fully actionable; length is not the signal. Use judgment about what the asker needed.

## Severity philosophy (non-blocking)
This is a formative habit, never a gate. Scale severity to how stuck the asker remains after the reply: a light nudge when the answer is nearly there but a pointer would land it; heavier when a real question is met with a reply that cannot be acted on at all. It never exceeds MAJOR on reply clarity alone. Describe the observable gap, never impute dismissiveness.

## Grounding and abstention
Quote the question and the reply you assessed. Return NO_REVIEW_OCCASION when the turn is not answering a question, when no question was actually asked, when the reply is a reasonable partial step in an ongoing exchange, or when there is no settled conversation to read. When a real question and its reply are both in front of you but the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether the answer had already been given elsewhere in it, return INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. Never fabricate an answer the reply did not give.
practices.whyItMatters: When someone asks for help, a reply that only gestures at the problem leaves them exactly as stuck as before and burns another round of messages. An answer with a concrete next step lets them get moving right away.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A reply that either solves the question outright or points to the exact next step or place to look, so the person who asked can act on it immediately instead of asking again.

practices.name: Post clear status and blocker updates
practices.criteria:
## The standard
Judge whether an update about ongoing work tells the team where things stand and, when the author is stuck, names the blocker plainly along with what is needed to clear it. A clear update lets teammates plan around the work or step in to unblock it; a silent stall, or an update so vague no one can tell whether help is needed, leaves the team guessing. Judge only the observable clarity of the update, never whether the work itself is on track.

## Good vs. bad
GOOD (PRESENT, GOOD): an update that states the current standing and, if blocked, says what is blocking and what would unblock it. BAD: an update on stalled or in-flight work that hides a blocker behind a vague line, or reports being stuck without naming what is actually needed, so no one can help. Use judgment; a brief "still on it, no blockers" among teammates already in sync is fine.

## Severity philosophy (non-blocking)
This is a formative habit, never a gate. Scale severity to how much the update leaves the team unable to plan or help: a light nudge when the standing is clear but the ask is fuzzy; heavier when a real blocker is present yet the update gives the team nothing to act on. It never exceeds MAJOR on update clarity alone. Describe the observable gap, never impute avoidance.

## Grounding and abstention
Quote the update you assessed. Return NO_REVIEW_OCCASION when the turn is not a status update, when there is no in-flight work or blocker to report, when the surrounding context already makes the standing obvious, or when there is no settled conversation to read. When an update IS posted but the thread you were given begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether the standing it omits was already established, return INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. Never invent a blocker the author did not mention.
practices.whyItMatters: When work stalls quietly, the people depending on it keep waiting without knowing anything is wrong, and a blocker someone else could have cleared in minutes sits for days. A plain update on where things stand and what you need keeps the team moving.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: An update that says where the work stands and, when you are stuck, names the blocker and what would unblock it, so teammates can plan around it or step in to help.
